newsitem.title: DUBAI: Pakistanis in UAE flock to aid economy at home.
newsitem.headline: Pakistanis in UAE flock to aid economy at home.

text.p: Pakistanis in the UAE, many of them poor labourers, are flocking to send money home in response to an appeal by Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif to help their debt-riddled economy, community leaders said on Tuesday.

Sharif on Sunday announced austerity plans to reduce foreign debts and called on Pakistanis abroad to send hard currency in the shape of donations, bank deposits and interest-free loans to the government.

"People have been very responsive," said Tanveerul-Islam Khawaja, head of the influential 300-strong Pakistan Business Council (PBC) which has organised a series of meetings in the United Arab Emirates on Nawaz's initiative.
He and others said they expected the over 300,000 Pakistani expatriates in the UAE to transfer between $100 to $200 million in the next few weeks.
Most of the money transfers are going into personal foreign currency accounts in Pakistan, thus boosting the country's international reserves.

After Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates is the second largest base for overseas Pakistanis, diplomats say. Some of them are top traders and bankers, but most are humble workers eking out a living.
"Many have confidence in Mr Sharif and feel he is the only one at the moment who can help solve Pakistan's economic problems," Khawaja, a leading travel agent, told Reuters.
Sharif, whose party won a landslide victory in February 3 elections, asked each expatriate to remit at least $1,000.
He accused past rulers of looting Pakistan for their personal benefit and burdening it with $30 billion in debts. Pakistan is following International Monetary Fund economic reforms.
Sajjad Ashraf, Pakistan's consul-general in Dubai, said the local Pakistani community had shown great enthusiasm about Nawaz's campaign to "remove debts, build the country".

"What has impressed me most is that people from the lower level of the community who cannot afford the $1,000 are willing to contribute smaller amounts and want to know how this can be done," Ashraf said.
A handful of affluent Pakistani businessmen in the UAE have already pledged to transfer millions of dollars home.
But many of the poor Pakistanis in the UAE say they might not be able to send more than 10 dirhams ($3.67) in aid.
"I have many mouths to feed back home," said Ahmed Farzan, a construction worker whose family of 10 lives on his 500 dirham monthly wage.

Habib Bank and United Bank Ltd, two leading Pakistani banks which have 18 branches in the UAE, said many of their Pakistani clients had contacted them seeking more information on Nawaz's appeal. Others had already sent money.
"Within the next two to three days we expect more momentum," said an official at one of United Bank Ltd's branches. He said the bank was expecting $20 million in transfers.

"In the last few days, $1.8 million were sent to Pakistan," added a Pakistani employee at Emirates Bank International Ltd which has nine branches in Pakistan. "Inshallah (God willing) we hope to support our government."
Nawaz, a former prime minister, has yet to name his government. ($1=3.67 dirhams)
